title: The Art of Dhak: The Heartbeat of Durga Puja
paras: Before you see the pandals, before you smell the incense, before you feel the crowds — you hear the Dhak. The thunderous, mesmerising beat of this ancient drum is the sonic signature of Durga Puja, an instrument so intertwined with the festival that one cannot truly exist without the other.

The Dhak is a large, barrel-shaped drum, typically about 1 to 1.5 metres in length, with a skin head on one end that the player strikes with two curved bamboo sticks called *kathi*. It is worn by a leather strap around the neck and rested on the player's forearm, giving them full mobility to walk, dance, and move as they play.

Its sound is enormous — deep, resonant, and thunderous at close range, carrying for extraordinary distances across the open air. When a dozen Dhakis play together, the sound is not merely heard but felt in the chest, a physical vibration that seems to reorganise the body's internal rhythm to match the beat of the festival.

The masters of the Dhak are the *Dhakis* — hereditary musicians who come primarily from the districts of Bankura, Bardhaman, and Birbhum in rural West Bengal. For most of the year, these men (and increasingly, women) are farmers or day labourers. But as October approaches, they dust off the drums that have been in their families for generations, tighten the skins, and begin the journey to Kolkata.

The relationship between Dhakis and Kolkata's Puja committees is ancient and symbiotic. The committees need the Dhakis to bring their pandals alive; the Dhakis depend on the festival income to supplement their agricultural earnings. A skilled Dhaki working the major festivals can earn enough in five days to sustain his family for several months.

What sounds to an untrained ear like exuberant percussion is, in fact, a highly sophisticated musical language with a precise grammar. Each phase of the Puja ritual has its corresponding Dhak sequence — its *dhara* (pattern or flow). The *Bhairon Dhara* plays during the morning worship, slow and stately. The *Sindoor Daan Dhara* accompanies the ritual of the vermilion offering. The *Aarati Dhara* builds in intensity during the lamp-waving ceremony, reaching a crescendo that seems to compress the distance between earth and heaven.

Experienced listeners — and most Bengalis become experienced listeners simply by virtue of growing up with the festival — can tell which ritual is being performed just by the rhythm emanating from a nearby pandal, even without seeing the ceremony.

In recent decades, a competitive circuit has emerged around the Dhak, transforming what was purely a ritual practice into a recognised performing art. The **Dhak Mahotsav** and similar competitions, held by cultural organisations and Puja committees across Kolkata and its surroundings, bring together the finest Dhaki teams to compete in front of judges and live audiences.

These competitions have dramatically elevated the prestige of the instrument and its practitioners. Young people in the Dhaki communities, who might otherwise have abandoned the craft for more financially secure professions, are increasingly taking pride in their heritage and seeking training to compete at the highest levels.

Perhaps the most heartening development of the last two decades is the emergence of women Dhakis. Traditionally, the Dhak was exclusively played by men — both because of its physical demands (it is heavy and requires significant arm and shoulder strength) and because of rigid gender roles in rural communities. But groups like *Saptashree* in Bardhaman have trained all-women Dhaki troupes that are now performing at major Puja events and competitions.

The sight of a woman in a red sari playing the Dhak with full-bodied devotion has become one of the most potent and moving images of the contemporary Durga Puja — a festival that honours a goddess of immense power, brought to life through the music of women who claim that power for themselves.

Former residents of Kolkata who have moved to other cities and countries describe the sound of the Dhak as the most powerful trigger of nostalgia — sharper than the smell of shiuli flowers, more visceral than any photograph. A chance encounter with a Dhak beat in a foreign city, at a Bengali cultural event, is enough to reduce a grown person to tears.

This is what great music does: it bypasses the intellect and speaks directly to the memory and the heart. And no music has ever spoken to Bengal's heart more directly, more insistently, or more lovingly than the ancient thunder of the Dhak.

title: A First-Timer's Guide to Pandal Hopping
paras: Pandal hopping — the beloved Kolkata tradition of visiting as many Durga Puja pandals as possible over the festival nights — is simultaneously exhilarating and overwhelming for the uninitiated. This guide arms you with everything you need to navigate the city's greatest festival like a seasoned local.

Imagine five consecutive nights where an entire city of 15 million people collectively abandons sleep, dresses in their finest clothes, and walks for miles through illuminated streets to marvel at extraordinary art installations housed in temporary bamboo structures. That is Durga Puja in Kolkata, and there is truly nothing else like it on earth.

If you're visiting for the first time, the scale and density of the festival can be intimidating. Where do you start? How do you move around? What do you eat? What do you wear? This guide answers all of those questions, and then some.

The five-day festival officially runs from Shashthi (the sixth day of the waxing moon) to Dashami (the tenth day), but the best nights for pandal hopping are **Saptami, Ashtami, and Navami** — the seventh, eighth, and ninth days. Puja committees release their dates weeks in advance; always check the official Puja calendar for the specific year.

The best hours? **9 PM to 3 AM**. By 9 PM, the crowds at most pandals have reached their peak atmosphere — the lighting comes alive, the music is playing, the energy is electric. Many Kolkatans don't eat dinner until midnight during Puja. Embrace this nocturnal schedule.
Forget your car. Kolkata's already chaotic traffic becomes completely gridlocked in the major Puja zones from Saptami to Navami. Your best options are:

- **Metro**: Kolkata Metro extends its hours during Puja, often running until 2 AM or beyond. It's the fastest way to move between North and South Kolkata hubs.
- **Auto-rickshaws and cycle-rickshaws**: Perfect for short hops between nearby pandals. Negotiate the fare before you get in.
- **Walking**: The most authentic option. Many of the best pandals are clustered together. Gariahat–Deshapriya Park–Ekdalia in South Kolkata, and Shyambazar–Bagbazar–Hatibagan in North Kolkata, are ideal walking circuits.
- **App cabs**: Available, but surge pricing is aggressive during peak hours. Book well in advance or be prepared to wait.
Every year brings new themes and new stars, but some committees are perennially worth visiting:

**North Kolkata:**
- **Bagbazar Sarbojanin** – The grand dame; traditional, dignified, architecturally magnificent.
- **Kumartuli Park** – Always adventurous in its themes; close to Kumartuli so you can walk through the potters' quarter.
- **Shyambazar Five-Point Crossing** – The crossroads illumination here is legendary.

**Central / College Street:**
- **Mohammed Ali Park** – Grand scale; the idol here is famous for its traditional beauty.
- **College Square** – Intellectual themes, right next to Presidency University.

**South Kolkata:**
- **Deshapriya Park** – Reliable artistry; always one of the most-visited.
- **Ekdalia Evergreen Club** – Boutique, carefully curated; beloved by art connoisseurs.
- **Tridhara Sammilani** – Bold and experimental; expect the unexpected.
- **Santosh Mitra Square** – Theatrical and spectacular; one of the city's most famous.
- **Sreebhumi Sporting Club** – Maximalist and spectacular; controversial and always trending.

Durga Puja is Kolkata's fashion show as much as its festival. Locals invest heavily in their Puja wardrobe — new outfits for each day. You'll see a magnificent mix of:
- Women in Tant and Kantha cotton saris, silk Baluchari saris, and contemporary fusion wear.
- Men in kurta-pyjamas, dhoti-punjabis, or smart casuals.

As a visitor, there's no pressure to dress in traditional Bengali attire, but wearing something festive will help you feel part of the celebration. **Comfortable shoes are non-negotiable** — you will walk many kilometres.
Durga Puja transforms Kolkata's streets into one vast open-air restaurant. You cannot leave without trying:

- **Phuchka** – Kolkata's version of pani puri, the undisputed king of street food.
- **Kathi Roll** – Flaky paratha rolled around egg and meat fillings, born on Park Street.
- **Jhal Muri** – A dry mix of puffed rice, chopped vegetables, mustard oil, and spices.
- **Mishti Doi** – Sweet yoghurt set in clay pots, available from every sweet shop.
- **Nolen Gur Sandesh** – Freshly made cottage cheese confection with date palm jaggery.
- **Ghugni** – Spiced dried peas, the perfect late-night snack.

1. **Charge your phone fully** before stepping out. Power banks are lifesavers.
2. **Download an offline Kolkata map** — data networks get overloaded in crowd zones.
3. **Carry cash** — many street vendors don't accept digital payments.
4. **Stay hydrated** — October in Kolkata is warm and humid. Carry a water bottle.
5. **Respect the sanctity of the puja** — when you approach the idol for darshan, observe the behaviour of devotees around you and follow their lead.
6. **Book accommodation early** — hotels near the major pandal clusters (Park Street, Gariahat, Shyambazar) book out months ahead.

title: The History of Kolkata Durga Puja
paras: Durga Puja in Kolkata is more than a religious festival — it is the defining cultural heartbeat of an entire civilization. Tracing its roots from royal aristocracy to the vibrant streets of the modern metropolis, the story of Kolkata's greatest festival is the story of Bengal itself.

The story of Durga Puja in Kolkata begins not in a temple, but in the courtyard of a zamindar's mansion. The earliest recorded large-scale Durga Puja in Bengal is attributed to Kangsanarayan of Taherpur, who is said to have organised a grand community worship around 1606 CE, spending a fortune equivalent to what would today be millions of rupees. But it was in Kolkata, the City of Joy and the former capital of British India, that Durga Puja transformed from an aristocratic ritual into the world's largest public arts festival.

Through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the wealthy Bengali barons — men like the Mullick family of Pathuriaghata and the Tagores of Jorasanko — hosted elaborate Durga Pujas in their palatial homes. These were private affairs, accessible only to invited guests and dependants, characterised by opulent feasting, theatrical performances, and elaborate idol decoration. The zamindari Puja served as much as a display of social power and munificence as it was an act of devotion.

The transformation from private to public — the invention of the *sarbojanin* (universal) Puja — is one of the most significant democratising movements in Bengali cultural history. Scholars trace the origins of the first community Durga Puja to Guptipara, West Bengal, in 1790, where twelve friends pooled their resources to fund a Puja none of them could afford individually. This model of collective subscription spread to Calcutta rapidly.

By the early twentieth century, para-based (neighbourhood-based) Durga Puja committees were sprouting across the city. The Bagbazar Sarbojanin Durga Puja, established in 1919, is often cited as one of the earliest and most influential of these community organisations. Inspired in part by nationalist fervour — the Puja became a space for community gathering outside the colonial gaze — sarbojanin Pujas were inherently political acts as much as religious ones.

The decades leading to Indian independence in 1947 gave Durga Puja a new, charged significance. The Goddess, who destroys evil with her weapons while maintaining a serene grace, became a potent symbol of the freedom movement. Pandals displayed imagery of Mother India as Durga. Poets like Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam wrote verses linking the divine feminine to the nation's struggle for liberation.

The Partition of Bengal in 1947, which drove millions of Hindu refugees from East Bengal (modern Bangladesh) into West Bengal, permanently altered the demographic and cultural fabric of Kolkata's Durga Puja. Refugee communities from Dhaka, Sylhet, Barisal, and Chittagong brought their own distinct Puja traditions, adding new flavours of music, cuisine, and ritual to the city's tapestry. Many of the most celebrated Puja committees in South Kolkata today were founded by these displaced communities, carrying their homeland in the form of their beloved festival.

The most dramatic evolution came in the latter half of the twentieth century when artist-intellectuals began transforming Puja pandals into experimental art installations. The *themar* Puja — themed Puja — movement, pioneered by artists such as Shilpi Tapas Ghosal and Pradip Das in the 1980s and 90s, broke every convention. Pandals stopped being mere decorated shelters and became immersive environments — recreations of medieval temples, social commentary installations, and tributes to endangered ecosystems.

Puja committees began competing not just on the grandeur of their idol but on the originality and execution of their artistic concept. The Chetla Agrani Club built a pandal from donated iron nails weighing several tonnes. Sreebhumi Sporting Club controversially recreated Las Vegas. Deshapriya Park made headlines with a pandal evoking the Notre Dame Cathedral. Each year's themes are debated, celebrated, and critiqued in newspapers, television studios, and social media with the seriousness given to major cultural events.

In December 2021, UNESCO inscribed Durga Puja in Kolkata on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity — a recognition that reaffirmed what Kolkatans had always known: that their festival is not merely local, but a contribution to world civilisation. The inscription acknowledged the Puja's extraordinary nature as a platform for community participation, artistic expression, and living cultural tradition.

Today, Durga Puja draws an estimated 45 million visitors to Kolkata over five days. The city's public transport system is stretched to its limits. Every hotel room within a hundred kilometres is booked months in advance. Celebrities fly in. Foreign ambassadors make their rounds of the major pandals. Artists, photographers, filmmakers, and writers descend upon the city. And through it all — the crowds, the commerce, the cameras — the essence of the Puja endures: a city coming together to honour the divine, to celebrate art, and to affirm community.

What makes Kolkata's Durga Puja unique is precisely its refusal to be a fossilised relic. It is a tradition that absorbs and reflects its times — addressing climate change through eco-friendly idols, celebrating marginalised communities through inclusive themes, and welcoming artistic experimentation while holding sacred the core rituals passed down through generations. The Puja is simultaneously ancient and breathlessly contemporary.
As long as the Dhak drums sound at dawn and the fragrance of shiuli flowers fills the October air, Kolkata will be Kolkata. And Durga Maa will come home.

title: Kolkata Street Food Trail During Puja Season
paras: During Durga Puja, Kolkata's legendary street food scene undergoes its most magnificent annual explosion. Every corner becomes a stall, every stall becomes a feast, and every feast becomes an act of celebration. This is your definitive guide to eating your way through the greatest food festival within a festival.

Kolkata is India's greatest food city — a bold claim that few who have visited would dispute. Its cuisine is built on the conviction that eating is not a necessity but a joy, not a refuelling stop but a ceremony. And nowhere is this philosophy more exuberantly expressed than during Durga Puja, when the city's already-prolific street food culture goes into overdrive.

For the five days of the festival, every footpath becomes a dining room. Tens of thousands of temporary stalls spring up alongside the permanent establishments, offering everything from age-old Kolkata classics to innovative festival-only specials. The smells alone — charcoal smoke, frying onions, bubbling oil, sweet condensed milk, sharp tamarind — create an olfactory tapestry as vivid as any pandal.

Nothing is more central to Kolkata's food identity than the phuchka, and during Puja it reaches its apotheosis. Kolkata's phuchka is fundamentally different from its North Indian cousin, the pani puri. The hollow spheres here are thinner and crispier; the filling is a mixture of mashed potato and spiced chickpeas; and the water — the crucial element — is a bracing, complex concoction of tamarind concentrate, black salt, cumin, green chilli, and fresh coriander that varies subtly from vendor to vendor.

The best phuchka stalls during Puja draw queues that stretch down the block. The vendors who become famous — and in Kolkata, celebrity phuchka vendors are a real thing — can serve hundreds of people per hour, each receiving their six hollow spheres with the practised, almost balletic efficiency of an assembly line.
**Where to find the best:** The area around Deshapriya Park, the Gariahat market crossroads, and the lanes flanking College Street are consistently cited by locals as the finest phuchka territories.

If the phuchka is Kolkata's soul food, the Kathi Roll is its most famous ambassador to the world. Born in the legendary kitchens of Nizam's restaurant on New Market Road in the early twentieth century, the Kathi Roll is at its simplest a flaky *paratha* wrapped around a filling — typically egg, chicken, or mutton keema with onions, chilli, and a squeeze of lime. At its most elaborate, it becomes a layered, multi-ingredient creation that requires both hands and several napkins to eat.

During Puja, roll stalls proliferate across the city. Every neighbourhood has its contenders. The question of which roll is the city's best is argued as hotly as the question of which pandal deserves the prize.

*Ghugni* — dried yellow peas cooked in a spiced gravy of ginger, garlic, tomato, and a dozen aromatics, served hot in a clay cup with a crown of finely chopped onions, green chillies, and a squeeze of lemon — is the essential late-night Puja food. It is simple, warming, filling, and carries the kind of complex spiced depth that rewards the cold-addled, tired pandal-hopper at midnight.

Look for ghugni stalls near major pandals, especially in the early hours of the morning when the bigger food establishments have shut down. The best ghugni is served by vendors who have been simmering the same pot since late afternoon.

Any Kolkata food journey is incomplete without a systematic tour of its legendary sweetshops. During Puja, the major *mishti* (sweet) establishments — Balaram Mullick, Bhim Nag, Sen Mahasay, KC Das — operate around the clock and produce extraordinary seasonal specials.

- **Nolen Gur Sandesh**: Made with the season's first date palm jaggery (*nolen gur*), this is a deeply aromatic, not-too-sweet confection with a complex caramel quality. Available only from mid-October.
- **Kheer Kadam**: A small ball of solid sweetened cream cheese (sandesh) encased in a layer of soft rasgulla-like outer skin, coated in khoya. Rich, layered, extraordinary.
- **Mishti Doi**: The ubiquitous earthen-pot sweet yoghurt, set with nolen gur during Puja season for an incomparable upgrade to the year-round version.
- **Pantua**: A fried version of the gulab jamun, darker, denser, and more intensely caramelised.

No guide to Puja food is complete without a mention of *bhog* — the communal feast offered by Puja committees to the Goddess and then distributed freely among devotees. The scale of bhog operations at major committees is staggering. The Bagbazar Sarbojanin Puja committee's Ashtami bhog, for instance, feeds tens of thousands of people.

The classic bhog menu is Sattvic — cooked without onion or garlic, as befitting an offering to the divine. It typically includes *khichuri* (a warming mung lentil and rice porridge), *labra* (mixed vegetable curry), *chutney* (sweet and sour, made with tomatoes or raw mango), and *papad* (crispy lentil wafer). Standing in a queue for bhog, receiving it on a sal-leaf plate, and eating it surrounded by thousands of strangers who are all, for that moment, your community — this is one of the most profound experiences Durga Puja offers.

During Puja, eat adventurously. Take the food that looks unfamiliar, buy from the stall with the longest queue (it earned those customers), eat standing up with a dozen strangers. Let the night run long. Order another phuchka. Try the vendor's special preparation that doesn't have a name on any menu. The best food in Kolkata during Puja doesn't come from restaurants — it comes from people who have been perfecting a single recipe their entire lives, serving it once a year to a city that loves them for it.

title: Kumartuli: Where Goddesses Are Born
paras: Tucked into the northern reaches of Kolkata, Kumartuli is a labyrinth of narrow lanes where the air perpetually smells of wet clay, paint, and incense. It is here, in cramped workshops passed down through generations of the Pal caste of sculptors, that the Goddesses of Durga Puja are born — one fistful of clay at a time.

Kumartuli — the "potters' quarter" — occupies a strip of land along the west bank of the Hooghly river in North Kolkata, its lanes so narrow that two people must turn sideways to pass each other. Yet within this compressed geography, an extraordinary miracle of human creativity unfolds each year between the months of June and October. Hundreds of artisans, primarily from the *Malakar* and *Kumar* (potter) communities, work feverishly to produce thousands of clay idols destined for pandals across Kolkata, Bengal, and increasingly, across the globe.

The neighbourhood's history stretches back to the late eighteenth century, when the zamindars of Calcutta began sponsoring grand Puja celebrations and required skilled sculptors to create their idols. Kumartuli grew organically around this demand, with the Kumar families who had long made functional earthenware pivoting to the more lucrative and prestigious business of idol-making.

The process of creating a Durga idol is a months-long journey that combines engineering, art, devotion, and ecological knowledge. It begins not with clay, but with a framework of bamboo and straw that forms the skeleton — the *chala* — upon which everything else is built. The straw is packed and bound to create the rough three-dimensional form of the Goddess and her accompanying deities: Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartikeya, Ganesha, and the defeated Mahishasura.

The clay itself is a carefully prepared mixture. At the heart of every Durga idol, by ancient tradition and now by practical necessity, is a small lump of clay collected from the doorstep of a *nishiddha pallis* — a brothel. The tradition holds that because the women of such establishments are considered outside polite society, the earth near their threshold absorbs the virtue that their visitors leave behind. This sacred, stolen earth makes the Goddess whole. It is a tradition that simultaneously acknowledges the marginalisation of sex workers and paradoxically includes them in the most sacred ritual of the year.

Layers of clay are then applied over the straw framework, smoothed, shaped, and detailed with extraordinary precision. The hands of the artisan carry centuries of muscle memory: the precise angle of Durga's chin, the exact curve of her ten arms, the positioning of her weapons, the set of her eyes — everything follows a canonical tradition while leaving room for the sculptor's individual artistry.

The most solemn moment in the creation of an idol is *Chakshudaan* — the gift of eyes. It is the final act of painting, when the sculptor draws the pupils of the Goddess's eyes. By custom and religious belief, this act is what animates the image, transforming an object of craft into a divine presence. Sculptors often fast before performing Chakshudaan and approach it with prayer. Once the eyes are complete, the Goddess is no longer a statue — she is real, she is present, and she must be treated as such.

The artists of Kumartuli work in conditions that have changed little over generations. Their workshops — often the ground floor of their ancestral homes — are small, dark, and densely packed. A single family might be producing forty, fifty, or even more idols simultaneously, at different stages of completion. Work begins before dawn and often continues by electric lamp long after dark.

The economics of the craft are brutal. The most celebrated master sculptors — men like Mintu Pal, Gouranga Pal, and Kartik Pal, whose work is sought by the biggest committees — can command significant fees and are treated with celebrity-like reverence. But the majority of Kumartuli's artisans work on thin margins, and many of their children are choosing other professions as the costs of raw materials rise and the fees paid by smaller committees stagnate.

Yet there are also signs of renewal. A younger generation of sculptors is experimenting with themes — creating Durgas that break convention, that make social commentary, that incorporate new materials. Women artists, long rare in Kumartuli, are increasingly establishing themselves. International orders — for Pujas in London, New York, Toronto, Singapore — bring new revenue and global recognition.

As Mahalaya approaches, Kumartuli reaches a fever pitch of activity. The lanes fill with flatbed trucks waiting to transport completed idols. Journalists and photographers crowd every workshop. Puja committees send their representatives to supervise final details and decorations. And through it all, the sculptors press on — touching up a colour here, fixing a drapery fold there, ensuring that every Goddess they send into the world is worthy of worship.

Then, within days of Mahalaya, the lanes fall quiet. The idols are gone. Kumartuli begins its long wait for next year, already planning, already dreaming, already shaping the Goddesses of 2027 in its collective imagination.

title: Sindoor Khela: The Bittersweet Farewell
paras: On the morning of Bijoya Dashami, as Durga Puja draws to a close, Bengali women gather at pandals across Kolkata for Sindoor Khela — a ritual of profound beauty, community, and bittersweet emotion. In smearing each other's faces with vermilion, they simultaneously celebrate love, womanhood, and the poignant farewell to a goddess who feels like family.

Bijoya Dashami arrives with a quiet that stands in sharp contrast to the preceding nights of noise and spectacle. The streets that teemed with millions of revellers are now tired, sun-dappled, and still. But at the pandals, a different kind of celebration is gathering — intimate, emotional, and exclusively feminine.

Sindoor Khela — literally "the play of vermilion" — is the final ritual before the Goddess Durga is carried to the river for immersion. Married Bengali women, dressed in their most beautiful white-and-red Tant saris, their own sindoor meticulously in place in the parting of their hair, gather at the feet of the Goddess. They offer her sweets, apply sindoor to the idol, and then to each other — smearing the brilliant crimson powder across each other's faces, hair, and white saris in an act of collective joy, solidarity, and sorrow.

In Hindu tradition, sindoor — red vermilion powder applied in the parting of the hair — is the mark of a married woman. Its colour evokes the blood of life, the fire of the marital bond, and the protection of the Goddess. When women apply sindoor to Durga on Dashami, they are treating her not as a distant divine abstraction but as a daughter-in-law returning to her celestial in-laws' home after her annual visit to her mother's house.

The mythology here is deeply human and specifically Bengali. In the imagining of Bengali Shaktism, Durga is Uma — the beloved daughter of the mountains, Himalaya and Menaka. Her annual five-day visit to her earthly parents' home ends on Dashami, when she must return to her husband Shiva's austere abode on Mount Kailash. The grief of Menaka, the mountain goddess watching her daughter leave, is a grief every Bengali woman understands — it is the grief of the parental home watching a daughter depart after the festival of marriage.

What transforms Sindoor Khela from a ritual into a phenomenon is its social character. Women who have known each other for years, and women who are meeting for the first time, participate in the same act of mutual adornment. The hierarchies of age, caste, and class that ordinarily structure Bengali women's lives are temporarily dissolved. A daughter-in-law can smear sindoor on her mother-in-law's cheek. Young women can embrace elderly grandmothers they barely know. The shared emotion of farewell creates a radical, temporary equality.

In recent years, Sindoor Khela has evolved significantly. What was once exclusively an activity for married women has opened its doors to all women — widows, divorced women, unmarried women, and women of other faiths and backgrounds have joined the celebration. Some of the most moving Sindoor Khela events in Kolkata are now organised specifically as inclusive gatherings, explicitly welcoming women who have historically been excluded from the ritual because of their marital status or community.

This evolution is contested — some traditionalists argue that it dilutes the ritual's specific meaning. But its advocates argue that the spirit of the Goddess, who is defined by her power and her compassion regardless of marital status, is better honoured by inclusion than by exclusion.

Every year, the most widely circulated photographs of Durga Puja are not the spectacular pandals or the illuminated streets — they are images from Sindoor Khela. The image of women covered in bright red, laughing and weeping simultaneously, pressing their foreheads together, holding each other tightly before the farewell — these images carry a charge that transcends cultural specificity. They speak a universal language of love, loss, community, and the passage of time.

The photographs taken at Sindoor Khela events at Bagbazar, Sreebhumi, and the Tollygunge Club have graced the covers of national and international magazines. They have been exhibited in galleries from London to Tokyo. They communicate something true and irreducible about human experience.

After Sindoor Khela, as the procession forms to carry the Goddess to the river, women wipe the red from their faces — slowly, reluctantly. The sindoor leaves a flush in the cheeks, a warmth that remains. They touch each other's feet, exchange sweets, and say *Subho Bijoya* — Blessed Victory — the traditional Dashami greeting that acknowledges both the triumph of the Goddess and the sorrow of her departure.
Then they go home, full of red and full of love, to wait for next year.
